questions.problem:
The entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ k & 6 & 0\end{aligned}]$
equals $18.$ Find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ k & 6 & 0\end{aligned}| & =1|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ k & 0\end{aligned}|+3|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ k & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(0-24)-2(0-4k)+3(0-k) \\  & =8k-3k-24 \\  & =5k-24.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{21}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(0-18) \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{12}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{21} \\  & =\frac{1}{5k-24}\cdot 18 \\  & =\frac{18}{5k-24}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{13}^{′}=18$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{18}{5k-24} & =18 \\ \frac{1}{5k-24} & =1 \\ 1 & =5k-24 \\ 25 & =5k \\ k & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Determine the entry ${a}_{13}^{′}$ in the inverse of a matrix $A$ $=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]$ if its determinant is $-4.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we want the entry ${a}_{13}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{31}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{31} & =(-1)^{3+1}|\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =15-(-1) \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{13}^{′}=\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{31}=\frac{1}{-4}\cdot 16=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The entry ${a}_{33}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & k \\ -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}]$
equals $\frac{1}{4}$ and $det(A)=6+3k.$ Find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, note that we are given the determinant of $A:$

$$
det(A)=6+3k
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{33}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{33}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{33} & =(-1)^{3+3}|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2-(-1) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{33}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{33} \\  & =\frac{1}{6+3k}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{1}{2+k}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{33}^{′}=\frac{1}{4}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{2+k} \\ 2+k & =4 \\ k & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in the inverse of the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ k & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]$
equals $\frac{1}{2}$ and $det(A)=2k+2.$ Find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, note that we are given the determinant of $A:$

$$
det(A)=2k+2
$$

Since we want the entry ${a}_{12}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{21}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{21} & =(-1)^{2+1}|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(0-2) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{12}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{21} \\  & =\frac{1}{2k+2}\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{1}{k+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we are told that ${a}_{12}^{′}=\frac{1}{2}$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{k+1} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ k+1 & =2 \\ k & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Determine the entry ${a}_{31}^{′}$ in the inverse of a matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$

${a}_{31}^{′}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =1|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}|-0|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\,(2+1)-0\,(0-1)+2\,(-0-2) \\  & =3-0-4 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since we want the entry ${a}_{31}^{′}$ in ${A}^{-1},$ we need to know the value of ${c}_{31}^{t}={c}_{13}$ in the matrix of cofactors. For this, we use the formula to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{13} & =(-1)^{1+3}|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =+|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-0 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since ${A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{31}^{′} & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{31}^{t} \\  & =\frac{1}{\text{det}(A)}{c}_{13} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}\cdot (-2) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$
